utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Three 92 bis witnesses today. They may or may not take all of the day. Can I just mention about four matters briefly to keep you in the picture about evidence or evidence difficulties, and may I mention the first three of them in private session because they concern witnesses and contacts with them and so on.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, we are in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: This relates to intercepts, several of which have been produced so far but only marked for identification and given different exhibit numbers. The Chamber will know that a witness is coming, and I shan't name him, in due course who can deal with these matters. No, actually my mistake. Perhaps we ought to -- I'm so sorry. Perhaps we ought to be in private session for this as well.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, we are in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, the witness, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: The Prosecution would call Ibro Osmanovic. Your Honours, this is an 89(F) witness which permission has already been granted for, so when he comes in, the statements will be presented in that manner.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. If the witness would take the declaration, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If you'd like to take a seat.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Agha.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: Mr. Osmanovic, you have given three signed statements to the Office of the Prosecutor, the first one on the 10th of October, 1994; second on 11th of October, 1995; and finally the third one on 7th of June, 2001. These statements will be placed before you. Can you please confirm that they have been signed and are in fact your statements?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, these are my statements.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: May I kindly ask the Court to please exhibit Mr. Osmanovic's statements.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit number is 597.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: Your Honours, this is a new municipality on which evidence I do not believe has been led as yet, so it may be helpful if first of all we went to a map of Bosnia just to show where this particular municipality is, if you would like to do that at this stage. The Exhibit number is actually 343, tab 1. And if that could kindly be placed on the ELMO so the witness could see it. It's also on page 29, D3 of your atlas, if that's of assistance.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: Now, the Prosecution has already led evidence regarding Zvornik and Bijeljina and other municipalities in Eastern Bosnia, and, Witness, could you kindly point out on the map on the ELMO Vlasenica municipality which you'll be dealing with.

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Vlasenica is here. It's in north-eastern Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: Indicate the municipalities of Han Pijesak and Bijeljina where you were detained in the at Batkovic camp.

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: I was not detained in the municipality of Han Pijesak but I came there. It gravitates towards the municipality of Vlasenica, and Bijeljina is by the Sava and by the Drina Rivers.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please be asked to spoke slower and to please speak into the microphone. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness. That is all with the map for the time being.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Osmanovic, did you hear the interpreter asking you to speak a little more slowly and into the microphone so they can follow what you say.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's no problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: So, Your Honours, if I may, I'll now read a brief synopsis of the witness's evidence. Now, the witness was living and working in the municipality of Vlasenica in Bosnia and Herzegovina in 1990. In 1991, he was selling drinks in Han Pijesak at a celebration when a group of JNA reserve soldiers from Vlasenica requested that the band play Serbian nationalistic songs. These songs have been banned in the former Yugoslavia because they were insulting to other nationalities. Some of these JNA soldiers were wearing Serbian national flag pins and Chetnik pins from World War II. The witness noticed that the Muslim and Serbian communities were beginning to divide. Between August 1991 and April 1992, the witness saw other similar incidents in other parts of Eastern Bosnia such as Sekovici. In Vlasenica, the Serbians and the Muslims also started to divide their communities. The witness saw on the TV Arkan and Plavsic in Bijeljina and the war in Zvornik. Everything was virtually calm in Vlasenica until 23rd, 24th of April when the JNA entered and took over the town. The JNA unit was from Novi Sad in Serbia and had tanks and armoured personnel carriers. The JNA took over the most vital departments in the town, which included the defence, police, justice, and the bank. The witness did not notice any Muslims in the JNA, only Serbs. The JNA demanded that everyone hand in their weapons, and if their order was not complied with, the town would be subject to force. After the JNA had taken over Vlasenica, it was turned into a Serbian municipality. The already existing Crisis Staff, headed by Milomir Stanic, moved from Milici and set up headquarters in the Boksit company which was in the centre of town. The witness believes that Milomir Stanic was in charge of all civil and military departments in Vlasenica with the commanders of the separate civilian authorities, including the police and military authorities, including camp guards at Susica camp, reported up the chain of command to him. The witness saw Stanic's name on many of the orders and movement passes. The witness believes that prior to the conflict, the SDS and the JNA were working together. The leader of the Serb special forces was a lieutenant in the JNA and he reported to Stanic. The SDS Crisis Staff and the Serb special forces shared the same headquarters in the Boksit company prior to the takeover. The Serb soldiers kept their same command structure and simply changed their uniforms. After the JNA takeover, a Serb friend of his was mobilising with the assistance of the JNA all of the Serbian men in Vlasenica. The witness saw the draft notices which his friend was preparing. These were documents on typed A5 sheets with the following heading on the left top: "Armed forces of the SFRY-SSNO Belgrade, 1524, VP, military post office Han Pijesak. Muslims had their movements restricted and they needed to get passes in order to move around Vlasenica. Muslims were also discriminated against in other ways. For instance, they lost their jobs, they were not paid their wages, and had restrictions on their bank withdrawal. When the JNA left on about 17th to 18th of May, they left all their equipment behind for the local Serbs who used this equipment to shell a number of nearby villages. The shells were incendiary and were designed to burn houses. The witness was arrested for the second time without being told why on the 22nd of May, 1992, and he was taken to the town police station where he was held in a room with 20 other Muslims. Whilst at the police station, he was severely beaten during interrogations with police batons, metal pipes, and metal chains. Whilst at the police station, he also witnessed a Serb policeman kill Mr. Ambeskovic who was a Muslim who had organised the referendum for a separate Bosnia and Herzegovina. On the 2nd of June, the witness was moved from the police station to the municipal prison where on arrival all his valuables were taken away. He was placed in a cell with ten other Muslims. The prison was designed to take 50, but there were in fact around 150 men detained there. Whilst the witness was at the prison, he was taken to the Muslim suburb of Drum in Vlasenica to bury bodies. He buried about 22 bodies. He personally knew four of the dead. All of the dead were adult men and had all been shot between the eyes, except one, from what appeared like close range. He was regularly beaten whilst he was at the prison, and numerous detainees were taken out and never seen again. He was later transferred on the 18th of June, 1992, to the Susica camp in Vlasenica. There were about 500 to 550 people kept at this camp. Only six or seven were women. The Susica camp was run by Dragan Nikolic, aka Yankee, who was a member of the Serb military special police. Nikolic told the detainees that he was God and law, and all the guards reported to him. The witness saw two of the detainees taken out of the hangar by Nikolic and who were beaten so badly that shortly after their return, they died from their injuries. He also saw a detainee named Reuf beaten so severely over the four- or five-day period that he begged to be killed. Nikolic, however, told him that a bullet cost three Deutschmarks. Nikolic also, in order to harass and intimidate the prisoners, fired his weapon over their heads, placed a pistol in the mouth of the detainees and continually beat them. On the 27th of June, a man with a JNA uniform with a major's insignia came to the camp and read out a list of people to be exchanged. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. The people boarded the buses, and a few days later, the witness also was taken to Batkovic where he arrived on the 30th of June. On arrival, he was immediately beaten by the guards. He also saw at Batkovic a 70-year-old man beaten to death. He was there for about 13 months. During this period, the witness noticed 10 to 12 detainees were singled out for particularly brutal treatment and beatings. This group was referred to as "the specials" and were kept apart. They were severely beaten several times every day. Alija, aka Konjanik, was in the specials group. The specials were beaten so much and so often that their faces became unrecognisable. Often they were beaten at mealtimes, so they had nothing to eat. Whilst at Batkovic camp, both he and other detainees were made to do forced labour, and they were also taken to guard abandoned Muslim properties in order to loot the property. Finally, the witness, after 13 months' detention at Batkovic, was released on 21st of July, 1993. Now, this is a short synopsis of the witness's three statements, and if I must -- might now, with the permission of the Chamber, just ask him one or two oral questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Osmanovic, you mention in your statement that the JNA took over town on the 23rd, 24th of April, 1992. Now, can you please tell the Chamber what the law and order situation was like in the town before the JNA took over.

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: It was the police station that maintained law and order in town. And there were no problems whatsoever, there were no armed conflicts, there was no mistreatment. There was just tension until the army came in. The army came in with combat vehicles and armoured vehicles. As soon as they entered town, they imposed a curfew, that is to say movement was restricted about town, the shops were not open. The next thing that was done was the following: A Golf police car was used for announcing to everyone over a loudspeaker that they should all surrender their weapons and that the army was there to guarantee the safety of all. However, after the hand-over of weapons, only the Serbs moved about, only the Serbs carried weapons, only their shops were open. But the Crisis Staff issued a statement to the Muslims that they should all go back to work otherwise they would lose their property that they had so painstakingly acquired over the years.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: Mr. Osmanovic, thank you, could I stop you there, please. I want now to come to the period where you were detained in Batkovic camp. Now, you mentioned a group of specials, one of whom was named Alija Konjanik. Can you tell us who he was and where he came from, this detainee?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Detainee Alija Konjanik was from Bijeljina. He was brought from the Bijeljina barracks to the Batkovic camp, having been accused of trying to throw a grenade into a cafe bar where the Serbs would gather, and they said that he threw this grenade off a horse. That's why they called him "The Horseman," Alija Konjanik. And the International Red Cross -- he was hidden from the International Red Cross and he was beaten by all the guards, and then he was taken to Doboj. After six or seven months spent in Doboj, he was returned to Batkovic and then he went to Tuzla.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, you mentioned the Red Cross coming to Batkovic camp. What happened to the children and elderly people when the Red Cross visited?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: In the month of August 1992, the Red Cross came, the International Red Cross came from Geneva to register these detained persons. This was the Batkovic collection centre, that's the camp I'm referring to. There was a group of very old men, over 65, and there was a group of children, and there was a group of a few of us able-bodied men, and they took us to the embankment on the Sava River by bus. And they took a group of specials by another bus to the farm. In our place, in place of the adults, they put the police. They took us there three days, as if we were going on a picnic, and after that they gave us documents as if we were -- had been registered by the International Red Cross, but for all practical purposes, we were concealed throughout that period.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: I just with the permission of the Court would like to show the witness an exhibit or two and see if he can comment on those.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Agha, if you would remember the clock, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours, absolutely. The first exhibit is at tab 4 of Exhibit number 597.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: And, Witness, if I could ask you very briefly to identify that place which you can see.

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: There is a hanger in this photograph. In very back, ammunition boxes can be seen. On the left and right-hand side are windows, but this is the hangar in Susica, in the Susica camp in Vlasenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: Was this where you were detained?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, But I was at the entrance, that is to say right by the entrance door.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, could the witness please be shown the exhibit which is found at tab 5 of 597 and kindly be asked to identify what he sees in that photograph.

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: The camp of Susica can be seen here. These prefabricated buildings are the forestry company from Vlasenica. The next prefabricated building is the warehouse of the Territorial Defence. In the period of 1992 it was used for storing military equipment. The next warehouse next to it is the hangar where the detainees were kept. That is also a warehouse of the Territorial Defence. What can be seen here is a room where the guards were. Over here is a truck. That's where the outhouse was, the toilet for the detainees of the Batkovic camp. By this -- by this river, which is also called Susica, was another toilet and then there is a road here and then this is where the gate was, and then this is where a pole was, the form of the letter A.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: If I may stop you there, Witness. That's fine. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: And I would apologise to the Chamber for providing black and white photos because -- to save the time, but I am finished now with my evidence in chief. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Osmanovic, I had available to me two statements. I did not have the third one, but that doesn't matter. You gave the first one in October 1994, and the second in October 1995; is that right?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Before that, you gave a statement to the Ministry of the Interior of Bosnia-Herzegovina to the service of state security in Tuzla on the 27th of July, 1993; is that right?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And you testified here on the 10th of October, 1995, in the case of Prosecutor against Dragan Nikolic, nicknamed Yankee; correct?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Have you ever been to Novi Sad or Sremska Mitrovica?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: I was in Novi Sad, yes. I have been to Sremska Mitrovica several times.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: On page 2 of your statement from 1994, in paragraph 5, you say that in Vlasenica things were quiet until the 23rd or the 24th of April, 1992.

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You say that's when the JNA arrived in Vlasenica.

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You said that on that occasion a motorised unit of the Novi Sad Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Corps from Sremska Mitrovica arrived in Vlasenica.

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: An armoured motorised unit armed with tanks and armoured personnel carriers.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: From the details -- from your details that I received, you did not serve in the army in Novi Sad or in Sremska Mitrovica but in Niksic, Montenegro.

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Military post box 6523.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could the witness be instructed to wait until the end of the question and speak more slowly, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Osmanovic, we've had another request from the interpreters. Could you speak more slowly and could you wait -- it's very difficult, I know, because it's -- you want to answer, but can you wait, when the accused has asked a question, until he's finished, and then you respond. Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You say on page 2, which is in fact the first page of the statement because the actual page 1 is cover page, you say those were soldiers of the motorised unit of the Novi Sad Corps from Sremska Mitrovica, and you said: "I recognised this unit because I served in the JNA from 1984 to 1985." Would you please tell me now if you did your military service in the JNA in Niksic, on what basis did you recognise the unit from the Novi Sad Corps, without going into where this unit had come from.

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: I recognised their weaponry. I didn't recognise the unit itself. I recognised the weaponry that only the army had available to it. Everyone knows what kind of weapons the army has, what kind of weapons the police has. This unit had tanks. And I know the unit was from Sremska Mitrovica, belonging to the Novi Sad Corps, because I met a young soldier from Bijelo Polje named Predrag. I talked to him and he said he was serving in the JNA doing his military service in Sremska Mitrovica.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. So this is based on what this soldier told you from Bijelo Polje. Bijelo Polje is actually in Montenegro, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Since you were talking about the corps, I understood you were saying that this unit was under the command of a lieutenant.

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: I just said the unit that was in town was commanded by a lieutenant.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: That's the only unit you saw, the one in town.

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: It was commanded by a lieutenant?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: You know very well that according to military strategy, every smaller unit is under the command of a larger unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I know that, but you are talking now about a unit of the Novi Sad Corps that you saw with your own eyes that was commanded by a lieutenant. It could only have been a platoon of soldiers if they were commanded by a lieutenant. It could not have been a corps or any sort of larger unit.

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, the six tanks that I saw with my own eyes could not have been a tank platoon. Six tanks could not be a tank platoon. And that number of soldiers walking about town who were everywhere around town could not have fit into the six tanks that I saw.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Let's clear this up. They were under the command of a lieutenant, and they were a unit of the Novi Sad Corps. According to you, where did this unit come from?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: In my opinion, Vlasenica bordered on Han Pijesak town which has a very strong garrison. It is a place populated by a majority Serb population. I know because I often went to Sekovici and Milici. I know that on the ground of the mine, the army was stationed, and in the factory of cardboard there were also army troops, and they could have arrived from three directions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, but all the three directions are on the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, but it's only 50 kilometres to the border. In the meantime, there were Serb forces already in Zvornik, as well as in Bijeljina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You know that neither in Zvornik nor in Bijeljina were there any JNA troops.

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: I would not agree with you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So you claim the JNA was in Zvornik and in Bijeljina?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: I assert there were people from Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I will not go into whether there were any people from Serbia. I know the JNA was not in Zvornik or Bijeljina.

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: The JNA was in Bijeljina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I noted here in your statement of the 10th of October, 1995, you said that from talking to some soldier named Predrag, you learnt that it was a unit belonging, as you say, to the Novi Sad Corps; right?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: That's precisely what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And you concluded that because he told you he was serving in Sremska Mitrovica during his military service?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And you did yours in Niksic, Montenegro?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: He told you he was doing his military service in Sremska Mitrovica, not that he was originally from Sremska Mitrovica.

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, he was doing his military service.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: He didn't tell you he had actually come from Sremska Mitrovica.

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And then by his accent, which became familiar to you when you were doing your military service in Niksic, you decided that he was from Montenegro, and he must have told you, I suppose, he was from Bijelo Polje.

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: He told me he was from Bijelo Polje.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And now, as far as I can see from your statements, because you are testifying according to your written statement, in your statement of the 10th of October, 1994, you said this soldier had told you the unit was under the command of this lieutenant whom you mention, named Musa, who was an ethnic Albanian.

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: That's what he told me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So this unit which we are not able at this moment to identify as a platoon or larger than a platoon was under the command of a lieutenant who was an ethnic Albanian. That's what you said in October 1994 in your statement, but you never repeated it in your later statements or testimony.

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: No, I did not. Nobody asked me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: They didn't ask you. I see. Well, then, Mr. Osmanovic, is it true that either then or later or today you cannot assert with any degree of certainty that this unit was from Sremska Mitrovica, and you cannot say from where it had arrived into your municipality? You say it was Vlasenica.

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I said it was Vlasenica. I stand behind what I said earlier, and I confirm it today, that it was a unit that I heard from the soldiers had been from Sremska Mitrovica.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All I heard you as saying was that this soldier was serving in Sremska Mitrovica. But let us move on to what is relevant. You say that this unit, it's again in your statement of October 1994, took over the main urban services in Vlasenica. "I saw them that morning taking over various services."

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: They took over the post office, that is communication, banks, the judiciary, the police station, the building of the hotel. And since I lived near the hospital, I saw them took over the hospital as well and put up guards outside these buildings; the municipality building, various companies and enterprises.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You say that they took over various services. Will you please explain, what did it look like, this takeover of urban services, municipal services? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: That's how I see the takeover of the military command, the court house, the municipal building, that is the town hall, where they put up guards as well as in front of the post office, banks, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. I was just trying to picture it and hear your explanation. But tell me about this putting up of guards outside important buildings. It was probably a slip of the tongue by Mr. Agha Khan when he side that they took over the Ministry of Defence in Vlasenica. You probably mean the Secretariat for Defence, the municipal Secretariat for Defence.

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, the municipal secretariat.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And you mean the municipal services. But tell me, when you saw them come and put up their guards outside municipal buildings, did the members of the JNA on that occasion mistreat or abuse anyone?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Members of the JNA walked about town carrying long barrels, that is rifles, and topographic maps, and in armoured vehicles there were people wearing masks or even without masks, and they were addressing announcements to the citizens of Vlasenica, that they should turn over their weapons and that the JNA was there to guarantee everybody's safety. In the event of failure to turn over weapons, the army would use force.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. That's not what I asked, in fact. What I asked you is this: When they arrived, when this JNA unit arrived whose size we cannot identify, did they mistreat or abuse anyone?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Apart from walk about town, I did not see them do anything like abuse or mistreat anyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: They just walked about town armed?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, soldiers are usually armed.

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Only in wartime.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: When they arrived, did anyone fire from their weapons? Was there any shooting?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: There was no armed conflict in Vlasenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So during the stay of the JNA in town, the unit did not mistreat anyone or use their weapons, firearms.

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: There was no mistreatment or use of firearms.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Were there any other reprisals that you could ascribe to the JNA units?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: There were reprisals that could be ascribed to that unit, such as appeal to go work as work obligation, then restrictions imposed on withdrawals of money in banks regardless of the actual amount of money that you had on your count, then the curfew which I also believe to be one form of mistreatment, restrictions of movement, and the appeal made to people who had left Vlasenica in the direction of Tuzla to come back lest they lose their jobs and property.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right, Mr. Osmanovic. If they were present there, if it had been announced on that occasion that they were guaranteeing everybody's safety, and if they appealed to everyone to come back to their jobs, wasn't that a step towards normalising life in Vlasenica if they were appealing to people to return to their homes and go again to work? Wasn't that a step towards normalising life in Vlasenica? And I want to be perfectly understood; I'm only speaking about the time when the JNA unit was present there. That's what I'm talking about. We'll come back later to the period when they were gone.

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: As far as whether this was a normal situation or not, it was not. That's what I'm going to say to you, because ethnic Serbs in the presence of the army carried weapons around town, whereas the Muslim people had handed over their weapons. They surrendered their weapons. So this was a modern-day camp. You're not armed, you're under fear of reprisals all the time, the only obligation you have is to work with your life in jeopardy.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What do you mean you have to work -- obligation that you have to go to work? It is only natural for people to go to work, to do the things they did before the war.

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, but whose safety did this army guarantee, to the Muslim people, for them to go back? But at the same time, they armed the Serbs. They allowed them to carry rifles, long barrelled rifles in town.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Osmanovic, isn't it correct that when this platoon or whatever it was, a unit larger than a platoon commanded by this Lieutenant Musa, an Albanian, when they were in Vlasenica and when they called people to go back to work and those who had fled from Vlasenica to come back to Vlasenica, when all of this was happening, wasn't their call addressed to all civilians for them all to return weapons?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So they said only the Muslims should surrender their weapons?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: That was the --

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Order.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Wait a second. Did you hear anybody from the JNA issuing this kind of order?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, in the vehicle that was driving about town and making this announcement, the Yugoslav People's Army guarantees the safety of all. The safety of all. But it calls upon the Muslim people to hand over their weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So that was the announcement?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Announcement.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: That is what you heard, that the JNA was guaranteeing everybody's safety and that only the Muslims were being called upon to hand over their weapons.

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: It is not allegedly; that is the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So they were not calling upon citizens, they were calling upon Muslims.

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Citizens of Muslim ethnicity.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So you've given me an answer. Thank you for that. Now, tell me, while this unit, this JNA unit was there -- or actually, how long was it in Vlasenica?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, roughly until mid-May.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Could you please be so kind as to remind me when they came.

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: April.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: The 23rd and 24th of April. So until mid-May, that was less than three weeks, approximately.

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And when did this unit leave? So it left in mid-May. Where did they go to?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: The tanks remained. Only the people got lost. They left town.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Oh, the unit left town.

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: The unit left town in terms of manpower, if I can put it that way, but the technical equipment was still there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So the JNA unit was there for three weeks, from the 23rd, 24th of April until mid-May. Now, I would like to ask you to answer me the following, because these are important questions for me. While this unit was in town, this JNA unit, did any -- was any citizen of Vlasenica arrested?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Hasan Kulanjcic was arrested on the 23rd and 24th as the army entered town. He worked in the furniture factory and then he was arrested and he spent all this time at the police station at the municipal prison in the camp of Susica and in the camp of Batkovic. On the 21st of July, 1993, he got out.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Let's not expand at this point in time. Let us not look at a longer period right now. So apart from this one man, was anybody else arrested over those three weeks while the JNA unit was in Vlasenica?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Some people were brought into custody. Some people were. And they were asked for weapons, and people from the party, from the SDA party were looked for, those who had organised the referendum. They were looking for things, and people were taken away for a day or for an hour or two. Some people were released after a day or two or three, but Dzevad Topalovic and Hasan Kulanjcic were there for years. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And who arrested them?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: They were arrested by the army when they took the furniture factory.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. But when the army left in mid-May, they didn't come with the army?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: No. They left them to the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So they remained in the prison where they had been before?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Was everybody hurt or killed while the JNA unit was in Vlasenica?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: I didn't see anyone being killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Was anyone hurt in any way, beaten up or whatever?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Hasan Kulanjcic was beaten, Dzevad Topalovic was beaten.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: While the JNA unit was there?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Who beat him? Because the JNA unit did not hold the prison, I assume.

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: I was there, Mr. Milosevic, to see who beat them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: How do you know that they were beaten while the JNA unit was there?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Because when I came to prison Hasan Kulanjcic did not have a single tooth.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: When did you come to prison?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: I personally saw Hasan Kulanjcic on the 2nd of June and I saw Dzevad on the 22nd of May.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You saw them and you were arrested after the JNA soldiers had left?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, four or five days after they had left.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Since there were no longer JNA soldiers there; right?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All of this that happened and that you're testifying about happened after the JNA left Vlasenica; is that right?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Both. Both.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What does "both" mean?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: It means that I have a statement that relates to the period before the army left town, and it also relates to the period after the army left town.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I understand. But while the army was still in town, or rather, this unit that was commanded by this lieutenant, these two men were arrested. You do not know about anybody having been mistreated while the JNA unit was in town; is that right?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. And tell me, please, while this unit, this JNA unit was in Vlasenica, was anyone's house torched or looted?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Three houses in Vlasenica were torched. The house of Fadil Tulkovic [phoen], commander of the police; of Huso Dautovic as well; and the house of a painter who's called Pekic, and that house is in the centre of town.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Who set these houses on fire?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know. I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. You didn't, but what do you think? Who did?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Knowing who moved about and the houses were torched in broad daylight and the fire brigade was prohibited from taking any action, then you can paint your own picture.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. I'm not even going to ask you about this. So no prison was established during the stay of the JNA there because these two men who were arrested while the JNA was there, these two men were taken to the regular police station, the prison.

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: No, in Vlasenica there wasn't any kind of prison, a regular prison or an irregular prison before the JNA came, but it was only after they came that one room on one particular floor was turned into a prison and also another room on the second floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I understand that. But you explained yourself that while the JNA was there, two men were arrested.

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Others were brought into custody but they were released too.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You say an hour or two?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: I also said a day or two.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And they were released and the police station, I assume, was not held by the JNA but police.

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: The police. Uniformed police, armed like any police would be, but consisting of Serbs strictly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'm not going into that. I'm talking about the JNA unit, the JNA unit did not hold the prison.

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: No, no, no. It didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So they had nothing to do with the prison?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: They didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. These calls to surrender weapons, all of this was done in order to prevent an inter-ethnic conflict of the local population in Vlasenica and a possible attack on the JNA that had already been customary; is that right?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: I would not agree with you. Mr. Milosevic, if one side is supposed to surrender weapons only and if the other side remains armed, then that is not prevention of conflict. I do not view this as conflict prevention; I see this as mere assistance to one side so they can mistreat and humiliate the other side.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: The army guaranteed the safety to all, and this safety would probably have been guaranteed had the decision not been made for the JNA to leave Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know, Mr. Milosevic, but the decision of the JNA regarding security, I mean, I myself am an eyewitness to the fact that I lost everything.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You didn't lose anything while the JNA was there. You lost all of that after the JNA had left.

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: But this is a decision that has to do with safety and security.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Since you lost everything, you lost it after the JNA had left, and you were arrested after the JNA had left.

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, but having trusted the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But the JNA had left, and all of this happened to you afterwards.

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: I trusted them, and when they left, the town was blocked, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: The army was compelled to leave Bosnia-Herzegovina, and they could no longer give you protection, as you know. But all right. Tell me something else now. Were there any inter-ethnic conflicts there between the Serbs and the Muslims while this unit, this JNA unit was present?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: No?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Isn't that the best proof of all that the JNA did not allow any conflicts?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: That is no proof, Mr. Milosevic, and it's not proof because, as for the municipality of Vlasenica, the local commune of Cerska did not want to surrender their weapons at all. They remained in their own territory, in their own village, for about a year after that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I see. I don't want to put any leading questions to you or anything. I don't want to suggest what you should answer, but I do bear in mind that when testifying here in the Nikolic case, you said that the JNA stayed there until mid-May and then you repeated that a few minutes ago, and then they withdrew to the area of Serbia, and now we have established that while the JNA unit was there there was no mistreatment of people. People were not killed, firearms were not used, and so on. None of these things happened in that period. You were first arrested towards the end of May, beginning of June; is that right?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: I was arrested on the 22nd of May.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: The 22nd of May. So this was at least a week after the JNA had Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. left.

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Four or five days after the JNA had left.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Witness, you are asked about your first arrest, not the second one. Was it on 22nd of May?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. The first time I was taken into custody from in front of the bank, and this was done by Stevan Muminovic. He brought me to the police station. They asked me then why I wanted to withdraw money from the bank, and then they released me and they did not mistreat me then.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: There is one thing that I would like you to explain to me, please. In your statement from the month of October 1994 -- I mean, I would like to ask you to try to remember and to give me the exact dates. In the October 1994 statement, as you were explaining when you were first arrested, you say, "After the departure --" This has nothing to do with your arrest but I'm just referring to this particular sentence in your statement. "After the regular JNA soldiers left, around the 5th of May, 1992, the reserve officers stayed on until the end of May," et cetera, et cetera. So regular JNA soldiers left already around the 5th of May; is that right?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: The regular army or, rather, the young soldiers -- I last saw them around the 5th of May. After that, I didn't see them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So regular JNA soldiers, according to this statement of yours, left already on the 5th of May?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So then on the 22nd, 23rd, if that unit came and if they left on the 5th, then they were not there even for a total of two weeks.

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: But I'm telling you again, regular soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'm not talking about different reservists now from a particular town and how long they stayed where they stayed, and they stayed on throughout as members of the army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: That is not true, Mr. Milosevic, that they stayed there throughout. They stayed there until they used the local -- they taught the local Serbs how to use tanks and mechanisation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But are talking about reserve officers who stayed until the end of May, nothing more, nothing less. Tell me something else, please. That means that already from the 5th of May onwards, 1992, there was not a single regular JNA member in the territory of Vlasenica.

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Conscript.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right, conscript. When were these two men arrested, as you said?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: The 22nd of April.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not hear the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So if the regular soldiers withdrew, then there were local people who remained.

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Local people and those who came with the regular soldiers, the older men who came with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, since you say that some vehicles stayed behind, where were these vehicles after the regular JNA soldiers had withdrawn? Where were they parked exactly, these vehicles?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: By the stadium in Vlasenica, the sports stadium in Vlasenica. There were three tanks that were parked there. Also in the Muslim cemetery. Right in the middle of the cemetery, that is where a tank was parked. One tank and one APC were moving about town.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All of this happened after the JNA left?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: While the regular army, while the conscripts who were doing their regular military service were there, there was one tank in the Muslim cemetery, and the rest were by the stadium.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. If they left these vehicles of theirs, how did they leave Vlasenica?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know how they left, but the vehicles stayed, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. We've clarified that. And then since the JNA withdrew, as you had put it yourself, you were arrested, and also a number of Muslims from the territory of Vlasenica were arrested as well; is that right? And then in your statement given to the investigators, you mention a number of names of Serbs who, according to your assertion, took part in the arrests and interrogations that had to do with the possession of weapons and also attacks against Serbian villages; is that right?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know anything about these attacks on Serb villages? Why did they ask you about that?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: We were asked whether we knew who had left for Cerska, where they had left, because in Vlasenica, there was no armed conflict. The first armed conflict began with the attack of the Serbs against Cerska. Cerska being an ethnically pure Muslim town, they did not allow the JNA to come in.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: When did that happen?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: In May.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: When in May?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, I don't know the date in May. But in any case, it was after the departure of the JNA.

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: At any rate, the conscripts from the army left.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You mean when the regular forces of the JNA left, that's when the attack against Cerska began?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me now, since you have enumerated some people, naming them, tell me now, among all those names that you have referred to - and I'm not going to repeat them - among all these people, was there a single person from the territory of the Republic of Serbia?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, from the territory of the Republic of Serbia there was Goran Viskovic, also known as Vjetar.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So one and one only. Where from?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: From somewhere around Ruma.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What about the others?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: From Tisca, Sekovici, Vlasenica, Han Pijesak, or Milici.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So there was one person from Serbia who happened to be there and the rest of the places that you named were places in your own area?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me now, please, because when you testified against Nikolic, you said that he was a member of the JNA.

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: He was armed with an automatic weapon of the kind that the JNA had. He wore a uniform of the kind the JNA wore. He drove a vehicle with JNA licence plates. What conclusion would you have come to?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But isn't it true that in response to the questions put to you by the side represented here by Mr. Agha Khan, you said that you had known Nikolic from before and that he was a local Serb.

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I know Mr. Nikolic from around town, from meeting him in the street, in catering establishments.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Well, that's all I wanted to know. He was a local Serb, a local resident. Is it true that he was employed as a civilian employee in the Alpro enterprise before the war?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: That is true.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did his brother work in the municipal administration?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, in the tax administration.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So we are talking about people who were local residents of Vlasenica.

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is it true that when testifying in the Nikolic case on the 10th of October 1995 you said that he was a member of a Special Police Unit of the Serb municipality of Vlasenica? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: I did say that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Why, then, did you ever claim that he was a JNA member? Is it just because he wore a JNA uniform? Those uniforms were all around.

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Uniforms perhaps, but not vehicles.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I am not challenging one or the other, but I want you to make your choice. Was he a member of the JNA or was he, as you yourself said, a member of the Special Police Unit of the Serbian municipality of Vlasenica? That's what I read in the transcript on page 24, lines 7 to 11.

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Dragan Nikolic, also known as Yankee, used to be employed in Alpro, the factory of aluminum pressings before the war. However, when the union of Serb municipalities was formed, Nikolic started going around wearing a camouflage uniform and carrying an automatic weapon. That's when I first saw him armed with an automatic rifle.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'm not interested in the details, I just wanted you to say clearly who he was. Since you say he was a member of a Special Police Unit, he could not have been a member of the JNA. Let us now clear up another thing, Mr. Osmanovic. You claim that you had been in some kind of camps. I wrote down Susica or Batkovic. Those are two different camps, aren't they?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Two different sites, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So we're talking about two different locations. We just saw a photograph where you indicated that it was the Susica camp. When was this photograph taken?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: We actually saw two photographs.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, one was an aerial photograph that does not show much, but the photograph where you see people, when was this taken?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know. But aerial photograph speaks to the exact location of the camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: The exact location is in the Vlasenica municipality; isn't it? And you don't know about the other photo, where it -- when it was taken?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I think it must have been made after the Susica camp was vacated, when everybody left.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In that big hall which you called hangar, I saw only a few people and the walls were lined with wooden or plastic ammunition or weapons cases.

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Those cases held weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And when you explained the other photograph, you showed us the warehouse of the Territorial Defence.

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So what does this photograph show us with a few people and some cases?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: It shows us the interior of the hangar.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And the people we saw there, were they detained or were they moving freely around the hangar?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know who these people were.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May, could we find out what kind of photograph that is and when it was taken? I don't understand what kind of exhibit it is if we don't know where it comes from and where it was -- when it was taken.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The witness has identified it as the interior of the camp. If there are any further details which the Prosecution have, no doubt they can give them after the adjournment.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. I won't go into it, but this is not the first time to -- we are presented with exhibits where you can see nothing at all. We can see big rooms with or without weapons inside them --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It doesn't matter. That is all to do with the weight of the evidence, nothing further.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. All right, Mr. May. I don't see how we can speak about any weight with this kind of evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, since you say you had been in these camps and I know nothing about it at all, could you explain to me one of the things you say in your statement. You say: "During my stay in Batkovic," you were beaten up. That's on page 14 of your statement. You said you were beaten up. "Fikret Smajlovic, Dzemal Zahirovic nicknamed Spajzer, and Esad Bekric, they were willing participants in the beatings because they beat other detainees with or without the guards presented. They seemed to be more violent or worse than the Chetnik guards." I suppose you remember this.

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: I remember this, and I will explain how it came about.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I want to know one thing: You are testifying here about the beatings, and from your own statement, it follows that the most brutal beatings were inflicted by Muslims themselves.

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: I kindly ask you, Mr. Milosevic, not to interrupt me. When we arrived on the 30th of June, 1992, on a transport that crossed Sekovici, Zvornik, and Bijeljina, in Batkovic we were first beaten up by Serb guards who happened to be there who also took all our valuables in the same go, beat us up, and then withdrew, leaving us behind locked doors. A few days later a group of people from Brezovo Polje, Brcko municipality, arrived, including Fikret Smajlovic, nicknamed Piklic. Dzemal Zahirovic, nicknamed Spajzer, came in the same group with me. How he arrived in Vlasenica, I don't know, but these two people before the arrival of Esad Bekric, nicknamed Beret, and also nicknamed Policeman --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let him finish. Let him finish. Yes. Go on.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] These three men moved about in the presence of guards, beat other people in the presence of guards, and these two, Fikret Smajlovic and Esad Bekric, wore uniforms and walked about around the hangar and the perimeter of the camp. Fikret Smajlovic, nicknamed Piklic, brought his own car. Where did you ever see a prisoner in a camp owning a car?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Not one.

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, this was one. So he enjoyed the support of the guards, the current command of the camp, and he was worse than many Chetnik guards. That's what I said, sir, and that's what it says in my statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, that's the only -- that's precisely what I'm saying, Mr. Osmanovic. While you stayed at that camp, you suffered the worst mistreatment from your own countrymen, Muslims, because we can see that this Fikret Smajlovic nicknamed Piklic, Dzemal Zahirovic nicknamed Spajzer, and Esad Bekric - you put a period here, you didn't mention his nickname - you confirm that those were the three worst men, all three of them Muslims.

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, in Batkovic camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And obviously they were not prisoners because you say one of them wore a uniform, arrived in his own car, so I suppose he was not a detainee. So the Muslims who were there were guards in the Batkovic camp. Isn't that right, Mr. Osmanovic?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: No, they were not guards. Mr. Milosevic, do not put words in my mouth that I did not say. Fikret Smajlovic came and went but he spent nights in the Batkovic camp in a bed specially arranged for him. Esad Bekric, "Policeman," also slept at the Batkovic camp. Spajzer was brought from Vlasenica together with me. He had been in the camp -- interpreter's correction: He had been in Vlasenica before. He came to the camp with me. He did not go out for walks. Fikret Smajlovic was the only one who wore a military uniform. The other one wore a camouflage uniform. I tell you, they were not guards. They were in the camp like me, but they beat other people.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All of them are without a doubt Muslims.

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Not all of them, only the three of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'm asking you about the three of them. And they inflicted the worst beatings.

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: I didn't say the worst. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: That's what you wrote here. Is it true that Braco Agic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We have been through this point and we have been on it for about ten minutes. It's more than enough. We can read and we can understand the point. It doesn't get any better by constant repetition, Mr. Milosevic. Yes, let's find something else to ask the witness about.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am not repeating. I am mentioning these other names for the first time. I mentioned three names.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But you say Braco Agic, Alija Ferhatovic, Bernes Hadzic, and Enes Hadzic, Klempic, and Nedzmin Aganovic were there. Is it true that Meho Kulanjcic, also a Muslim, put salt on the wounds of another Muslim? Not one but many Muslims.

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: He put salted compressed for swellings to subside.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What about the other people I named?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Those are Muslims from Vlasenica whom Dragan Nikolic, nicknamed Yankee, left outside the hangar when the doors, when the gates of the camp close to monitor and to watch for family members of the detainees who would come to bring food to the detainees and to prevent them. Those people were his informants.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So they were prisoners, but at the same time informants who mistreated other prisoners.

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: They did not mistreat them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What did they do?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: They just informed on them to the camp commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: To the warden.

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: He was not a warden, he was camp commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is it true that your entire statement that you gave to the investigators on 11 October 1995, that is one day after your testimony in the Nikolic case, is dedicated to the mistreatment you suffered in the Batkovic camp? In fact, this mistreatment you ascribe to this Piklic, Spajzer, and Esad Bekric, it seems to me.

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: You don't mention Veljo, Zoran, Gligor, Major, and the rest.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I read out to you an entire paragraph of your statement. I did not omit a single name from the paragraph. I cannot read out loud the whole statement. I just wanted to establish that the worst mistreatment and beatings were inflicted to you precisely by your fellow Muslims while you were in the Batkovic camp.

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: That's what you say.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I was quoting you. I'm not saying anything.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. There's no point continuing this argument. Now, you'll move on to something else. You've got six minutes left, Mr. Milosevic, and we're going to adjourn now. Twenty minutes, please. Mr. Osmanovic, would you remember not to speak to anybody about your evidence during this adjournment, until it's over. Yes. We will adjourn.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May, I will continue now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In relation to uniforms, you did your military service, didn't you, and you had this same JNA uniform; right?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Wasn't it a generally known fact throughout Yugoslavia that all reservists had JNA uniforms?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So these who were on the police force or on the reserve force, they all had these JNA uniforms, they all wore JNA uniforms that were available to them all that time, even before the conflicts broke out; is that right?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Just one more question that has to do with Cerska. You said that in Cerska there was a unit of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Who was there? Who was that unit or, rather, were these the Green Berets?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know who it was, but I know that in Cerska it was the people who organised themselves. They did not allow themselves to fall under the influence of the so-called army and the Serb forces. As for the Green Berets, Mr. Milosevic, I never saw them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Patriotic League, something like that?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Never saw them, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: How big was this unit in Cerska?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know who commanded this unit?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You don't know the number of people involved? You don't know who was in command? You know nothing except there was one Muslim unit in Cerska?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I don't know the number of people involved, Mr. Milosevic, but I know that there was one unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And it managed to survive for all of one year, as you said.

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: From 1993 to Cerska-Konjevic Polje when the enclave of Srebrenica was formed, the people, including a group that my mother was in, through Cerska and Crni Vrh, they came to Tuzla.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Were these units under the command -- under the command of Naser Oric there in the enclave of Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know who was the commander in Cerska but Srebrenica is 60 kilometres away from me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And how far away is Cerska from you?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: 30 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So how can you know anything about what went on in Cerska and what happened in Cerska?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: My mother was a prisoner at the Susica camp. My sister was a prisoner at the Susica camp. One sister and another sister. One sister never came back from Susica. Whereas my mother and one sister were transferred to Cerska.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: That is to say territory that was under the control of the Muslim forces.

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. They were allowed to go to Cerska and then on the 3rd of February they came to Tuzla, in 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: When were you exchanged?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: I was exchanged on the 21st of July, 1993 in Kovanica.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, how many people were exchanged then, how many Muslims from your side?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: You mean from the camp of Batkovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I don't know what camps these were but how many were exchanged then?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: From the camp of Batkovic, about 400 men were exchanged.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And who were you exchanged for? Did you manage to see?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: I saw people going both ways. On the one side there were men from the Batkovic camp, on the other side were people who had come from Tuzla, and then I went to Tuzla.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: These who came from the other side, they were Serbs who were exchanged; right?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Were they soldiers or were they civilians?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: I did not see any soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So you were exchanged for civilians?

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: I was exchanged for a civilian, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. No further questions.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. May.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Just one issue, Your Honour. Looking at page 68 of the first statement of the witness. There's no need for the statement to go before him as it's a simple matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Page 68? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Sorry, paragraph 68.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Witness, in your statement you refer to the changing of the uniforms after the Serbs took charge in Vlasenica. Could you explain what that change was.

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: The change of uniforms when the Serbs took over power and authority in Vlasenica, this consisted of the following: The local Serbs wore red -- white ribbons on their lapels, and also, before, the JNA had a Red Star on their caps but now there was a typical Serbian flag.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: If you could describe that flag, what you mean by "a typical Serbian flag."

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: The flag that was there before was the three-coloured flag with a red five-pointed star. On the caps there was only a red five-pointed star, and then the caps had these stars taken off and a flag was put there, blue, red, white, which was for a while the flag of Yugoslavia and for a while the flag of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a clarification.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Blue, white, red is the flag of Yugoslavia. I assume you know that.

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And Serbia is blue, red, white.

utterances.speaker: IBRO OSMANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, this is just the order in which the colours are placed. I'm not going to that, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Agha, would you deal with this matter quickly.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: I have no re-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. Mr. Osmanovic, thank you for coming to the Tribunal to give your evidence. You are now free to go.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, let me deal with one administrative matter. There was a question at the last hearing which Mr. Tapuskovic raised, namely to have the minutes of a session of the Presidency admitted, Exhibit 328, tab 16. In fact, that was all admitted previously, and so there's no need to be admitted again. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I can just deal with that. It had been served only in English on him and not in B/C/S. So that's why he misunderstood.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I have always understood that Mr. Tapuskovic's records of exhibits are amongst the best of the various parties -- not the Chamber, of course, but amongst the rest of it, amongst the best kept. May I raise one other small administrative point. Perhaps I can deal with it in private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, we're in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. If you'd like to take a seat.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: May the witness be handed the statement in English, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Witness, look at the first page of that statement. Are your personal details identified on that first page?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1746
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Witness, your signature appears on the first page of that statement. Is it a statement that was taken on the 5th of April, 2000, and again on the 20th of April, 2002?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1746
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Subject to some points of difference which I'll deal with, are the contents of that statement true to the best of your knowledge and belief?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1746
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Your Honour, I ask that the statement is admitted under Rule 89(F) and be assigned an exhibit number. It was the subject of an application that was granted last week by the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. The exhibit number, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Under seal.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, the next Exhibit number is 598 under seal.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: I'll read a summary. The witness is Muslim of Bosniak ethnicity and from Doboj municipality. She lived in a village called Miljkovac, about three kilometres from Doboj town, and will describe the attack on the village and on Doboj town and the situation in Miljkovac and in the municipality of Doboj generally before and after the attack. She describes Doboj as a mixed municipality of about 25.000 people with about 49 per cent of the population being Muslim. The witness's village was majority Muslim.
