The witness describes in her statement the various JNA facilities in Doboj municipality. The main JNA barracks was located in Miljkovac about a kilometre from where the witness lived. It was a huge training facility, and the witness drove between the two parts of it every time she went home. There were also military buildings in the villages of Sevarlije and Potocani and training fields in the villages of Putnikovo Brdo, Plane, and Prisade. The witness says she knew that weapons were being distributed to Serbs in Doboj in late 1991. When the war in Croatia began in 1991, she noticed many Serbs were absent from work, either on a military training exercise or gone to fight the war in Croatia voluntarily. In March or April 1992, the witness saw soldiers digging trenches and placing cannons outside the JNA military facility near her village. In April 1992, she began to hear shootings at night in nearby villages. She began to notice many private cars driving around with no registration plates. Soldiers in these cars were wearing camouflage uniforms and red berets. It was common knowledge that they were from Serbia. They were stationed at the JNA barracks close to the witness's home. The town was full of them. The witness saw them looting and burning houses in the neighbouring village of Plane. The witness says that regular Serb soldiers were afraid of the Red Berets. She heard that when regular soldiers tried to escape fighting on the front line, the Red Berets would tie them in trenches to prevent them escaping. In May 1992, what the witness describes as ethnic cleansing by Serbs calling themselves Special Forces, Red Berets, and White Eagles started in Doboj. They wore camouflage uniforms as opposed to the regular JNA military uniforms worn by reservists. Muslims and Croats started leaving the area because they were scared. The Red Berets, White Eagles, and Special Forces committed many crimes. Men were arrested and taken away, women were raped, and there was a lot of looting in the town. The witness identifies the various detection facilities in town. She describes the detention facility at Cafe Perco and beatings carried out by Red Berets there. She describes detainees being transported to perform forced labour at the front line. Doboj was attacked on the 2nd of May, 1992. The municipal buildings were taken over by the Serbs. The witness describes the shelling which she heard as she hid in her cellar for the next seven days. Approximately four or five days later, Serb Special Forces came house-to-house, searching for weapons. They were wearing camouflage uniforms and had black paint across their faces. They came to the witness's house looking for money and electrical equipment. The witness describes life in Doboj after the attack. A curfew was imposed. Serb soldiers would come regularly to search their houses. Former rubbish collectors were used to gather the bodies around town. The witness describes the arrest of her husband in July 1992 and his subsequent detention at the main JNA barracks and at a camp with hangars near the Bosanska juice factory. The witness and her family finally left Doboj in November 1992. Your Honour, I have a couple of points on clarification that I'd ask the witness. Your Honour, if we may go into private session briefly.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, we are back in open session.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Witness, look at paragraph 45, please, of your statement.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1746
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: The Special Forces you identify there as having carried out house-to-house searches, can you tell us, please, if they were wearing any head gear.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1746
utterances.text: They wore black berets, and their faces were painted with some kind of black paint. It looked as if they were masked.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Did those men say anything about what they were doing in Doboj?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1746
utterances.text: They didn't say anything. They just asked us to give them weapons. They searched houses. They were looking for technical equipment, but they did not tell us why they were there.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Turn, please, to paragraph 21 of your statement. You describe an attack on the village of Plane. Are you able to say or describe who it was who attacked that village?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1746
utterances.text: The village was attacked by the Serb soldiers, as it says here.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Tell us, please, those soldiers that attacked the village, were they wearing any head gear that you observed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1746
utterances.text: Most of these soldiers wore red berets, and they were driving cars of the Golf make but without any licence plates.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Your Honour, those were the only additional matters I had to raise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do not have the number of this witness. I cannot find it, because she is protected, and I cannot address her by name since she is a protected witness. Could you be so kind as to tell me her number.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness 1746, since I have two of your statements, one given on the 5th of April, 2000, the other given from the 5th to the 20th of April, 2000, I will, when asking questions, refer primarily to your second statement, which gives more detail, and I will indicate when I refer to your first statement to make this examination more simple. So in your statement, in paragraph --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter didn't hear which paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Page 3 you describe a harmonious life in your community where you used to live very well until 1992.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1746
utterances.text: That's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I do not doubt that. But in the middle of paragraph 4 on page 2 you say, describing the economy, you say: "Looking back now --" that is paragraph 5 "-- I know now that the most important positions were given to Serbs. The Muslim population was never interested in that sort of thing and just didn't care." I want to ask you, did somebody tell you this later or is it your direct firsthand knowledge?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1746
utterances.text: That's the way it was, because all the major, important positions Serbs used to get by using their connections, family connections and otherwise, distributing these posts among their cousins, uncles, and extended family starting from schools and enterprises. I'll give you one example. In the place where I used to live, in my company until 1981 or 1982, the factory mostly employed Serbs. However, in the 1980s, a new director was appointed, a Muslim, and it was then that the number of Muslim employees started to grow.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But you say yourself that it was mainly Serbs who used to work in that factory and that a Muslim was appointed general manager, which is exactly the opposite of what you said a moment ago - namely that the Serbs occupied the most important positions - if a Muslim was appointed director of a factory employing mostly Serbs.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1746
utterances.text: This happened in the period while a Serb was the general manager. Muslim workers could simply not get jobs there until 1981 or 1982, when the number of Muslim employees increased.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. You gave me a good enough explanation. Can you give me at least one more example, because the one you just described is very clear. What are the most important positions that you say were held by Serbs?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1746
utterances.text: Well, starting from the Yugoslav People's Army to managerial positions such as general managers, heads of departments, foremen, whereas the simplest and the worst jobs they were simply not willing to take.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you really think that in a harmonious mixed community there could exist really such a difference between ethnic groups, that the Muslim population was not interested in important positions and that was some sort of their nationalist -- national characteristic, whereas Serbs were keen to hold important positions and were ambitious, and that was their national characteristic? Isn't that a trait of individual character?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1746
utterances.text: I'll give you just one example. A person who used to work as a janitor at the reception desk went to an evening training course, and after that received promotion into head of section.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, that was a very common occurrence in Yugoslavia, for people to receive additional training and be promoted. I don't think it has anything to do with ethnicity. I don't believe that ambition is a national trait.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1746
utterances.text: I can agree with that. What I'm saying is that many people applied but were not employed on that position, whereas this simple janitor did become head of section.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't believe this was a factory that involved high technologies, the factory you are talking about. It was not a factory that used state of the start technology.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1746
utterances.text: It doesn't matter now. It's just an example I gave you. I myself applied for different positions on various occasions and was rejected always while a Serb was the general manager, and then when the Muslim became general manager, Muslims and Croats applied and got jobs because they were judged not by their ethnicity but by their actual qualifications.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. In paragraph 7 of your statement you said you heard and saw on television that Karadzic was often visiting in the area of Mount Ozren, both before and after the election. And then you link that to the fact that the Serbian army set up their headquarters in a place called Preslica very close to Mount Ozren. If I understand you well, you want to say that Serbs were preparing for the war, and that's why Karadzic went there.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1746
utterances.text: The Serbs were not preparing. They were already prepared.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, don't you know that the majority population near Mount Ozren is Serbian and that is the logical explanation?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1746
utterances.text: I know that. That's why they chose it as their main base.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But don't you think that the majority Serbian population was the reason why Karadzic went there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1746
utterances.text: All of this was organised, because war could not have started in just two months. Before April and May -- you know how long it takes for the former Yugoslavia to be transformed into Greater Serbia. Your countrymen, members of the Serbian ethnic group, said this publicly, and I had opportunity to see it for myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: They were saying publicly that Greater Serbia is being created?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1746
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Ma'am, I won't ask you any more questions about this, because you said you were not very political, you didn't even vote. From all that you said in your statement, we can see that you were minding your own business most of the time, which is an entirely different story. That's why I want to know, how come you know that the Serbian headquarters were in Preslica near Mount Ozren? Don't you know that there was no headquarters there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1746
utterances.text: No headquarters?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, all right. How do you know that there was headquarters there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1746
utterances.text: The entire Doboj, with its environs, was the base of the Serb army.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you mean some kind of local command for Doboj and its surroundings? It wasn't headquarters or anything.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1746
utterances.text: All I can tell you that -- is that Mount Ozren was and remains a Chetnik stronghold. Nowadays, after the war, I think the aspiration to create a Greater Serbia lives on, and most probably if there are enough vicious people, what happened a couple of years ago can still happen again and not only once.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. You say in paragraph 8, page 2, that in November 1991 at election time it appears that everyone voted mainly for the nationalist parties. Don't you know when the elections were actually held?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1746
utterances.text: This may be a mistake, but I know for a fact that everybody voted for nationalist parties.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What you mean is that Muslims voted for the SDA and Serbs for the SDS.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1746
utterances.text: Precisely.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And then you say that after the elections, Serb symbols with four letters S appeared and Serbian children started singing Serb songs.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1746
utterances.text: Precisely.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What does it mean if Serb children sing Serb songs? Is that a sin?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1746
utterances.text: No, it isn't a sin, but if they do so in public places -- if somebody calls me a great Muslim or calls you a great Serb, then that is not all right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: We're talking about very old Serb songs, and you said yourself Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. that the song "We Are Alija's Army" was sung.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1746
utterances.text: I mentioned this because I didn't agree with it. It has a nationalist connotation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: It does, and it's not a traditional song. It is a reference to the army of Alija Izetbegovic that was established recently, whereas Serb songs had been sung for centuries.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1746
utterances.text: No, not in the former Yugoslavia. At least not in public places.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Given the significance of this witness's evidence, is there really any significance on what songs were sung 12 years ago? You criticise the witness for not knowing the date of an election 12 years ago and then you ask questions which really cannot have any significance in my view. Let us move on and find something more significant.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, Mr. May. I will find something that you will consider relevant.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 5 on page 3 - and I'm only referring to the statement of the witness who is testifying on the basis of her written statement - you speak about the disbanding of TO units, and you say you don't know what happened to their weaponry, and then you say, "Later during the conflict I found out that Serbs had taken over the weapons in order to distribute them to Serbs."

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1746
utterances.text: That's the way it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You don't know -- you didn't know, in fact, you later found out. You found out from whom?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1746
utterances.text: I found out from a man who worked with me, a colleague of mine, who said loud and clear that they always came by night, around midnight or after midnight, and knocked on doors of Serb houses and distributed weapons to them. If somebody did not want to receive a weapon, they were threatened. The same happened to those men who refused to go into the reserve forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Do you know that there was an order of the former authorities of Yugoslavia withdrawing weapons that had been kept in TO warehouses all over Yugoslavia, not only in Bosnia-Herzegovina but in Macedonia, Slovenia, and every other republic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1746
utterances.text: I am aware of that, and I know the reason for that order. It was designed to prevent those weapons from being taken over by Muslims and Croats, and those weapons were kept in the barracks of the former JNA. However, Serb troops, soldiers of Serb ethnicity, got hold of these weapons later.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that the Serbian TO also had to give up their weapons in the same way?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1746
utterances.text: I didn't understand your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: The same thing was done in Serbia. The weapons of the Territorial Defence were put in the hands of the JNA.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1746
utterances.text: I know that. But I also know that all the plans that were developed, including plans for war and attacks on parts of the former Yugoslavia, were made in the Republic of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: How could you possibly know that? Tell me, please.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1746
utterances.text: Well, that was very well known. When your own parliament fell apart - I don't remember in which year it was - when you quarreled in your parliament and before the war you started making, what do I know, plans for dividing the parties of the former Yugoslavia with one part going to Croatia, another part going to Serbia, another to Bosnia and Herzegovina --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I would really like you to enlighten me. Which parliament are you talking about? What happened there? Who was making plans to divide Yugoslavia into various parts that were to be divided among Croatia, Serbia, Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1746
utterances.text: I did not put that in my statement, but I will say it now, because I know. All your conferences in Serbia, Croatia, and Bosnia, when you met with Tudjman and Alija Izetbegovic, you always failed to agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: There were meetings involving all presidents of Yugoslav republics, and the last of them was held in Stojcevac, if you remember.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1746
utterances.text: Well, I was not that interested, so I don't remember the time and the place, but I know that you participated in the carving up of a country and of one people.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, you certainly could not have derived that conclusion from those meetings, because we were committed to preserving that Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1746
utterances.text: Yes. You were committed to preserving that Yugoslavia which was actually to be Greater Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So that is what you mean.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I'm going to stop this debate. This is merely a debate on general issues. It has nothing to do with the witness's evidence. Yes. Move on to more concrete matters, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I agree, Mr. May, that what the witness is replying has nothing to do with her evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So you say a large number of Muslims and Croats were leaving.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. Pack has something. Yes?

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: I was concerned that the accused is going to be asking questions which may lead to the identification of this witness. If he could be cautious of that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll make an effort.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, you must be careful about that sort of thing.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am very careful, Mr. May, especially when such lady witnesses are concerned, and I've never made a mistake of this kind until now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: "We did not know or understand why they were leaving." So from January to the spring of 1992, a great many Muslims and Croats were leaving the area. You were naive. You did not know why they were leaving. So this is the time before the war broke out, when negotiations were held in order to overcome the crisis and to avoid a war. What is it that the Muslims and Croats knew at the time and what you did not know because you were so naive?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1746
utterances.text: They seriously took the war in Croatia. They took the war in Croatia seriously, and they were leaving probably because probably they were better informed than I was. They realised that this war would reach Bosnia as well. And all of this was done systematically, town by town.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But you say the Serbs took it in order to divide it up among the other Serbs. That's what somebody told you. Somebody said that to you; right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1746
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So you're not testifying about what you know, you are testifying about things that other people told you.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1746
utterances.text: I testify about things that other people told me and about things that we know because we did not have any access to these weapons. And had we had access to weapons, the situation would have probably been different.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Oh. So that means that to the best of your knowledge, the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, as the armed force was called, the one under the command of Alija Izetbegovic, it was not armed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1746
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Oh. It was not armed; right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1746
utterances.text: It wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Very well. Then you say in paragraph -- or, rather, on pages 3 and 4, you say that in 1991, both Serbs and Muslims were Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. receiving call-up papers to join the JNA and that the Serbs did respond, but the Muslims, and I'm quoting you: "Nobody responded to the call-up." That's what you said. "Nobody responded to the call-up."

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1746
utterances.text: First and foremost, the Muslims and Croats remained at their workplaces. Hardly any of them were called up as reservists for this military exercise, and it was mostly Serbs who went as reservists because they had to go, because they were receiving threats. They were threatened by imprisonment if they did not respond.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I assume that you know that the law was the same in the former Yugoslavia. And it's not only the Serbs who would have gone to gaol if they did not respond to the call-up, Muslims and Croats would have too. But you say no one, none of the Muslims and Croats responded.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1746
utterances.text: They didn't because when the war broke out in Croatia, many Muslims did respond but then they were sent to the front line.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Do you know that the Party of Democratic Action was calling upon the Muslims not to go into the JNA?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1746
utterances.text: I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So what do you think? Why did no Muslims respond? Why did this happen? How could this happen?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1746
utterances.text: Because most of the call-up papers were sent to citizens who were ethnic Serbs. And secondly, people already felt unsafe, and a minority was getting call-up papers. I just know of one case. A colleague from work who received call-up papers to join the reserve force did not go. He was supposed to go to Preslica.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I see. That is where the Serb headquarters was, as you had put it.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1746
utterances.text: Precisely.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And this was actually a place where the Territorial Defence rallied.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1746
utterances.text: Whose Territorial Defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: A Muslim got call-up papers and did not go there.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1746
utterances.text: In that area, the Territorial Defence could not function.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Wait a minute. The man who was called up, was he a Muslim?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1746
utterances.text: Precisely.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And then he was supposed to go to this place that you call Serb headquarters. So it was the Territorial Defence that was being called up regardless of whether they were Serbs or Muslims. Isn't that right, Mrs. 1746?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1746
utterances.text: He got call-up papers but he refused them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I understand, because you say that none of the Muslims responded.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1746
utterances.text: I said loud and clear that he did not respond and for the most part it was Serbs who responded because they had to go there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I understand. But this Muslim who received call-up papers was called up to go to the place that you call a Serb headquarters and this was actually the focal point of the Territorial Defence of the municipality of Doboj. Is that right or is that not right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1746
utterances.text: I'm just going to give you one example. A few people were taken up there to Preslica, and they've been missing since then.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You heard about that; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1746
utterances.text: That was in the newspapers and on television. A few people lost their lives for no reason whatsoever because somebody thought there was a reason for that. Let me just say one more thing: These were citizens who were ethnic Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right, Mrs. 1746. On page 4, in paragraph 4 you say in the beginning of April you started noticing soldiers in privately owned Golf cars without licence plates, in camouflage uniforms, and so on and so forth. You say that everybody knew they were from Serbia because you say, "We could not recognise them." The fact that you could not recognise them, could that mean that they were not from your area only or how can this mean that they were precisely from Serbia?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1746
utterances.text: No. These people were from Serbia. We knew that. And they themselves made it known that they were coming from Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, what they were making known could be a completely different matter. But do you know, since you are talking about Golf cars without licence plates, that it was precisely in Sarajevo, in Vogosca, that the Golf car was manufactured? Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1746
utterances.text: Are you trying say that these were soldiers of Muslim ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Madam 1746, I'm not trying to say anything. I'm just trying to put a question, and I ask you kindly to answer my question. Do you know that it was precisely in Sarajevo -- rather, in Vogosca that there was a manufacturing plant of Golf automobiles?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1746
utterances.text: As far as I know -- I actually do not remember. I know there was a factory, but I do not remember. I wasn't really interested in that kind of thing. But let me just tell you something else: That these cars, these Golf cars were in front of the garrison in my town.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I don't know where they were. I just know that these vehicles of the Golf make were manufactured in Sarajevo, in Pretis. That's the name of the factory. Also, that from the storage space of the Sarajevo factory, many of them were stolen. I assume that you would know that they were not stolen by the JNA but, rather, by local inhabitants, and they drove them in all directions. So those were the cars that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The witness can't possibly know all this. We've heard the evidence about it, and I don't think the witness can take it any further as to where these cars came from. All she can say is that these were the cars. If you want to call further evidence about it, you can.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right, Mr. May.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 4 on page 4, you say that these soldiers were not regular Serb soldiers. That's the way you put it. And then you say they themselves said that they were members of the special forces of the Red Berets or White Eagles. Is that what you say?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1746
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And in paragraph 4 on page 5, you say: "At the time in Doboj there were only volunteers from Serbia, rather, members of the Red Berets, White Eagles, and Serb volunteers from Bosnia and Croatia as well as those from Romania and Russia."

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1746
utterances.text: Yes. There were a lot of mercenaries.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So you saw these different volunteer groups. And how did you distinguish between and among them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1746
utterances.text: I could recognise the regular army of the former JNA, I could recognise the soldiers with red berets, and I could recognise the soldiers who called themselves the White Eagles. These were paramilitaries.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Paramilitary forces.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1746
utterances.text: Yes, paramilitary forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: No doubt about that, that the White Eagles are paramilitary forces. Now, tell me something else. How did you manage to identify these groups from Romania and Russia and so on? How did you come up with that? This is the first time I hear of any volunteer units from Romania and Russia.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1746
utterances.text: Didn't you hear about them on television and over the radio, that people from Russia and Romania came to fight in Bosnia for very small amounts of money on the side of the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I didn't not hear this on radio and television. Perhaps this was on some radio that you listened to. And also, you say didn't I hear this over radio and television. Did you actually hear this from radio and television?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1746
utterances.text: Precisely.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You didn't see them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1746
utterances.text: Well, I didn't see them, fortunately.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Let's not go into this any further. You talk about things that you actually did not see. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Recently a witness was here, a French journalist, and he brought pictures of the members of the White Eagles, and they had red berets on their heads. So what is the difference in terms of the caps they wear, the members of the White Eagles and those who called themselves the Red Berets, as you put it? Is it the same group or are these two different groups?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1746
utterances.text: We or, rather, I saw quite clearly, and I would encounter them from February, March, until May 1992. I had the opportunity, actually, of seeing every day the Red Berets and also the regional army, the Serb army, and these members of the White Eagles. Finally, some of them wore red berets, others were black berets, and yet others wore ordinary caps but without the red star, the red five-pointed star. That's a well-known fact. Some of them had red or yellow ribbons on their shoulders and that's how they could be identified.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. In your statement dated the 5th of April, you say on page 2 in paragraph 4, I'm quoting what you say: "There were some men with insignia of Arkan's White Eagles. They had camouflage uniforms but on their shoulders they wore different insignia so they could be recognised.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1746
utterances.text: Sir, these White Eagles were where I lived so I had the opportunity of seeing them every day.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Does that mean that White Eagles and other volunteers were dressed the same way or in a similar way as others and then it was necessary for them to have this special kind of insignia on their shoulders?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1746
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, is it that important what people wore?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: It's not that important, absolutely. But I would like to identify what you are testifying about and what you actually saw, because you say here, verbatim, "There were some men with the symbol of Arkan's White Eagles. It is generally known here that Arkan's soldiers were the Serb volunteer guards.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1746
utterances.text: Yes, and they had --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But the Eagles had nothing to do with Arkan. How did you come up with this, that Arkan had the White Eagles?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1746
utterances.text: Well, you had so many paramilitary organisations that no one can know all their names.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, paramilitary organisations do not belong to the states, as you know, so it's not that we had them. They were paramilitary organisations. So isn't it quite clear that the White Eagles and Arkan's volunteer guard were not one and the same thing? You claim here that it is the same thing.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1746
utterances.text: For us -- I beg your pardon. For us, it was the army of the Republic of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right, Mrs. 1746. Since you're talking about Arkan's White Eagles, I had to put a question in that respect. I did not ask you about any army of the Republic of Serbia because there was no such thing. There was the army of Yugoslavia, as you know full well, I presume.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Your Honour, might the accused identify the paragraph to which he's referring as the reference to Arkan's White Eagles. I can't find it in the statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, he doesn't have the numbers. Perhaps you could look for it over the adjournment. Yes. Let's keep going.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Is there any other statement of this witness?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can tell you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just a moment. Yes, tell us.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have already pointed out at the very outset that I would say specifically when I refer to the first statement. So I said specifically the statement dated the 5th of April, 2000, and I quote from page 4. "There were men with insignia of Arkan's White Eagles. They wore camouflage uniforms, but on their shoulders, in order to be readily recognisable, they wore different insignia." So this is the second paragraph on page 4 of the statement dated the 5th of April, 2000.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Let's move further on. In paragraph 5 on page 4 you say that the regular Serb soldiers were afraid of those you call the Red Berets, because the latter beat them, as you said. And you repeated it also during the very brief examination-in-chief you had here. They forced them to fight at the front line, and you heard that they even tied them up in trenches so that they would not flee from combat.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1746
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: How is this possible? Soldiers who are supposed to fight at the front line are tied up by someone in trenches so that they would not flee from combat? How can they fight if they are tied up? How can a soldier who is tied up fight? How did you get these ideas?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1746
utterances.text: Well, we're not going to be so very literal. It's not that they were quite literally tied up. I mean, their hands were not tied up.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Oh, their feet were tied up?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1746
utterances.text: Well, they were tied one to another in the trenches. And that's how they found Serb soldiers. And they were reservists for the most part, ordinary men who were in the trenches. All paramilitary troops or, rather, the army of the Republic of Serbia and the regional army of the JNA were for the most part stationed in town. They looted most of the time and searched houses and committed crimes, whereas normal, ordinary soldiers were in the trenches.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What does this mean in your vocabulary, this regular army of the JNA? I cannot understand this. I cannot identify what you mean by this "regular JNA" or "regional JNA," depending on what you say.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1746
utterances.text: The former Yugoslav army of the former Yugoslavia, because you know that at the beginning of the war there was no more Yugoslav army. It was divided. The Serb army, the army of Serbia or -- and then there was the army of the Federation and the army of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. These regular soldiers, when you use that word "regular soldiers" as the ones that you refer to, were they members of the regular army of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1746
utterances.text: Yes, they were. Of Republika Srpska, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So we've clarified that point, at least. In paragraph 7 and 8 on page 5 of your statement, you say: "Reservists freely moved about in military uniforms of the JNA and with full gear. There were many new faces in town. It was known that Serbs wore camouflage uniforms whereas our local reservists wore regular military uniforms of the JNA." These local reservists of yours, the ones that you refer to, and regular Serb soldiers that you refer to, are they one and the same thing or not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1746
utterances.text: I can just say that in the beginning just when the war began, they had normal old olive-grey uniforms. But after a month or two, for the most part everybody had camouflage uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Oh. So these same people, members of the army of Republika Srpska that you talked about a few minutes ago. First they had olive-grey uniforms and then camouflage uniforms.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1746
utterances.text: Yes, but we know what the army of Republika Srpska was and what the army of Republic of Serbia was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: The Republic of Serbia does not have an army. I don't know how you identified the army of the Republic of Serbia. Do you mean the JNA?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1746
utterances.text: We know that with the beginning of the war, the Yugoslav People's Army ceased to exist. The only army that existed was the army of the Republic of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1746
utterances.text: I will not go into this and make you suffer these questions. Just tell me this thing: In the last paragraph on page 4, speaking of the Doboj Red Cross, which in May 1992 was located in the secondary school of Doboj, you say the following: "In May 1992, the Red Cross was located in the secondary school of Doboj. It was the Serb Red Cross. And throughout the war, nobody worked there. In the beginning, Serbs used it as a refugee camp where food was distributed to displaced persons. Later, it was used as a detention centre. I know that prisoners were kept and Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. tortured there because I used to go there to visit them, bring them coffee, and clothing. The brother of my aunt was detained there" - I'll skip his name - "her son, one and the other." I will not name anyone for your safety. "And they were later exchanged." Now, regarding this quotation, will you please tell me who are these people who had been expelled to whom food was distributed in that centre? Where did they come from and who expelled them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1746
utterances.text: Well, first of all, it was a school.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I quoted you, Madam 1746. I quoted your statement very precisely. You did not clarify that it was a secondary school. I refer you to your own statement, and I'm asking you to tell me: Who are those expelled people you mentioned to whom food was distributed in this refugee camp? Where did they come from and who expelled them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1746
utterances.text: There were both Muslims and Serbs among the expelled people.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So there were both Muslims and Serbs who had been expelled and food was distributed to them. Where did they come from and who expelled them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1746
utterances.text: Well, Muslims were expelled by Serbs, as we all well know. And as for Serbs, they had left their homes even before the attack.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And who expelled the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1746
utterances.text: I don't know who expelled the Serbs from Bosanski Brod, because Bosanski Brod, as far as I know, belongs to Republika Srpska, and it must have been attacked by either Croats or Muslims, because we know that Bosanski Brod is located on the border between Bosnia and Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So when Bosanski Brod was attacked, Serbs fled and that's where they were accommodated; right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1746
utterances.text: Precisely.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Because you say it was a Serb Red Cross. Food was distributed, and the refugees were Muslims and Serbs. Doesn't that mean that food and assistance were given to everyone?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1746
utterances.text: I just wish to point out that it wasn't only the Red Cross headquarters. One part of that facility was a detention centre where Muslims and Croats were tortured.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: As you explain now, it seems to have been some place of torture.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1746
utterances.text: Precisely.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And you say that those alleged detainees were exchanged.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1746
utterances.text: Yes, they were. In 1994, I think, they were exchanged, because I saw a couple of the former detainees after the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So Muslims held Serb prisoners, Serbs held Muslim prisoners, and they later exchanged them; correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1746
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now tell me -- I'm not going to identify anyone. I'm not even

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1746
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me now, if you said just before that, and I quoted you, that nobody worked in the Red Cross throughout the war and it served as a detention camp, why did you ever go there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1746
utterances.text: We had to go there for purposes of identification and registration, because by that time we were refugees ourselves. We were forced to leave our homes and to report to the Red Cross base where we received some sort of registration slips that had our names on it. Briefly, we were registered there. After that, we left. We did not stay there for a long time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, that means that the Red Cross did work, did operate after all. You said on page 4 that it didn't. From what follows -- it follows from what you just said that it did work. You received some documents there and that's what you just explained, isn't it? Isn't it, Mrs. 1746?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1746
utterances.text: Just give me a moment. On page 4 I can't see this passage.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Page 4, and I'm going to speak about the Doboj Red Cross, you said that in May 1992, the Red Cross was located in the Doboj secondary school. It was a Serb Red Cross, and nobody worked there. So first you say nobody worked there, and then you say that you went there to get registered.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Perhaps I can assist --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What actually happened?

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Perhaps I can assist with the paragraph number. It should be paragraph 26 on the witness's copy.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: My apologies to the witness, because I am not quoting the numbers of the paragraphs because I received the numbered version only a moment ago. The one I was using until now did not have any numbers.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1746
utterances.text: Let's me answer this question now. "In May 1992, the Red Cross was located in the Doboj secondary school. It was a Serb Red Cross, and during the war nobody worked there." What I meant was that it no longer operated as a school. There was no more teaching staff or any other employees and that the Red Cross was stationed there with their own staff doing their own work.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you for this. Now, speaking about the detention of your husband, paragraph 10, page 4 of your statement. I want to ask this question before we adjourn for a break. It is not a short paragraph, and please pay attention, because I want to make a comparison. You say: "The prisoners were mistreated, and they hardly got any food all day. They had to sleep on pallets. On one occasion, I managed to bring some food to my husband and give it through a guard through the fence for it to be given to my husband. He never received it." That's what it says in that paragraph, whereas in paragraphs 8 and 9 on page 7 of the statement given in 2000, you say: "They were mistreated, and they hardly gave them any food all day. They had to sleep on pallets. I managed to get" -- And you say this very clearly: "I managed to get some food to him every day through the fencing around the camp." These are two different assertions, Mrs. 1746. Which of the two is true? Did you manage to get some food through to him on one occasion or every day?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: All right. We have the question. What we don't have is the numbers of the paragraphs. The witness can perhaps think about that -- just a moment -- can think about that over the adjournment. Ms. Pack, you will please find these paragraph numbers for us, locate them.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We'll adjourn now. Witness B-1746, when we come back, we will give you the right numbers of the paragraphs and you can have a look at them before you answer, because you should at least know what the accused is referring to. Could you remember, please, during the adjournment not to speak to anybody about your evidence until it's over. Yes. We will adjourn. Twenty minutes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May, if I may assist the witness, please. I said, actually, that my first quotation comes from page 4 -- in fact paragraph 4, page 9. And my second quotation is from paragraphs 8 and 9 on page 7 of the statement dated the 5th of April. My first quotation is from the other statement, and the second quotation is from paragraphs 8 and 9, page 7 of the statement dated the 5th of April. So she knows the exact location of these paragraphs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We only have one statement, as it is. We will have it clarified after the event, and then, Mr. Milosevic you've got ten minutes more for cross-examination. Yes, I'll sign the form.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Ms. Pack, have you the answer for the conundrum?

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Yes, just to clarify in relation to the statements, there is an earlier document headed "Witness Information" that wasn't signed by the witness. It was just a record of the first interview which then was followed by a second interview two years later, at which point the witness signed the statement that you see before you, Your Honours. So far as the paragraphs which -- to which the accused has been referring the witness, I can just explain. The first paragraph in the second statement, it's at paragraph 71; and in the first draft I've identified the relevant paragraph for the witness on the version in -- which is in front of her. Should Your Honours wish to see the first draft, I have got copies to pass up to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Witness B-1746, if you've got those paragraphs now, the accused's question was about an apparent discrepancy about whether your husband received the food or not. Perhaps you can deal with that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The first statement that I gave in the year 2000 is one that I did not sign because the computer broke down, so I could not read the statement out. So then ever since there have been some small mistakes that we corrected while it was being translated. I can say that it was only on one occasion that I managed to get some food to my husband. As for the other times, never. I never managed to do that again. I can also tell you, and perhaps this has to do with that, I went to the camp every day in order to visit him, if possible, to visit and see my husband.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May, since this witness undoubtedly requires a bit more patience during her examination, I don't think I can finish within ten minutes, so please bear with me. As for the fact that the statement was not signed, on page 8 it says "Witness acknowledgement" and then there is a signature and the date the 5th of April. There is no difference whatsoever compared to the other statement where it says the date the 20th of April and then there is a signature. Neither one actually bear a signature. It just says "witness's signature."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Milosevic, I am here to give you only the real kind of evidence, true evidence. It is not in my interest to lie to anyone and to say things that are wrong.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So what is written here on page 7 of that first statement of yours: "I managed to bring him food every day and to give it to him through the fence," that is simply not correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1746
utterances.text: That is not correct. I managed only once, but I went there every day.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: On page 4 of your statement, in paragraph 6 you said, and now I'm quoting you: "In May 1992, the Serbs started cleansing Doboj ethnically and that the Muslims and Croats, out of fear, started leaving the area." That is a quotation. And on page 6 - so we're talking about one and the same statement here, the one that you signed - on page 6, paragraph 9, speaking of the Serb takeover of Doboj on the 2nd of May 1992, you say the following: "After seven days an announcement was made over the radio addressed to the workers telling them they should all go back to their workplaces. I was not called up, but my work -- my husband was, and all of those who had taken anything from -- anything from their companies were supposed to take them -- these things back. When my husband went back to work, he had a new boss, a Serb." Mrs. 1746, this is where I quoted you. Does that mean that the Muslims and Croats were not expelled from Doboj? On the contrary; they were called upon to go back to work, just like the Serbs, but some of them left out of fear.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'm asking you about what you said here. "After seven days, there was an announcement made on the radio asking workers to go back to their workplaces."

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1746
utterances.text: Yes. Radio Doboj said that workers, I mean individual workers, who had material resources from their companies, they were supposed to go back and to hand them in. My husband was under this work obligation for about seven days, I think, and then he was released. He went home. There was no more work for him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So what it says here is not correct, that after seven days an announcement was made asking workers to go back to their jobs.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1746
utterances.text: Well, don't misunderstand what I'm saying. There are some workers who worked for the public cleaning company, and they had to sweep the streets and do whatever they were supposed to do. And other -- Serb workers took up arms and went to fight. So Croatian and Muslims workers had to work at the public utility in charge of cleaning and sweeping.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'm not going to go into all of that any more, although that's not the way you put it. You said in your statement that people were called upon to go back to their jobs. Tell me, on page 4, in paragraphs 6 and 7, when speaking about what you call ethnic cleansing which started in May 1992, you say: "The Red Berets, the White Eagles, the Special Forces committed a great many crimes. We did not dare go out during the night, and for the most part we stayed at home. Men were arrested and taken out. There was a lot of looting in town. Women were raped." And then you proceed to say -- these are all quotations from your statement. "One night around 1.00 a.m., we were returning from a visit we paid to a friend, and by the barracks in my street we came across a large concentration of military vehicles. Every day the activities in the military barracks went up." Now, isn't this quite contradictory? In one paragraph you say that you did not dare go out during the night, and already in the next paragraph you say that you were returning home at 1.00 a.m. from a visit that you paid to a friend and you passed by the barracks, no more no less, with a large concentration of military vehicles and stepped up activity. So were you locked up in your homes during the night or did you stroll by the barracks at 1.00 in the morning? Not both can be true.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1746
utterances.text: The answer to your question is the following, Mr. Milosevic: Well, it all was not in the same order. This is what happened in April 1992, while the war had not broken out yet, and we could still go and visit people, and people could come and visit us, and we could move about freely. However, in that period there was a large concentration of military vehicles and of military forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: That was not my question. My question was that in one paragraph you say "We did not dare go out," and in the second paragraph you say that you were strolling around at 1.00 in the morning by the barracks.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1746
utterances.text: Yes, but in one paragraph there is a description from the war days, if I can put it that way, and this other paragraph involves April 1992, and at that time, war had not broken out yet. However, when the war did start, we did not dare leave our homes, we did not dare go out into our yards after 11:00, and we did not have a chance to go to town or anywhere else.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Well, take a look at this now. In the one but last paragraph on page 6, you say: "A curfew was imposed straight away. From 8.00 until 11:00 there was restriction of movement. Those who were found after a particular time in their own yards were arrested and taken to the barracks at the end of the street." And afterwards you say: "The curfew was gradually extended. It was extended to 1500 hours, at the beginning of June we were allowed to stay outside until 1900 hours." I don't understand any of this. Could you please explain what kind of a curfew is this in the morning and afternoon hours, and when did this curfew start or, rather, end? 8.00, 11:00, 1500, 1900 hours. You refer to all these different times, so --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1746
utterances.text: During the first month we were not allowed to move about. The curfew was from 8.00 to 11:00.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In the morning?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1746
utterances.text: Yes, in the morning. We only had three hours to go to town or to go back home. However, in the months of June and July, as you said, they extended the time we had available for moving around. So in July and August, during the summer, we could stay outside even until 7:00 in the evening. I mean not stay outside but go to a shop, buy things if we managed to find anything, and then we'd have to go back home.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right, Mrs. 1746. On page 7, paragraph 3, you say: "I never saw a killing myself, but I heard that when the town was taken, some men were killed in their houses and some women were raped." So as for all the killings that are referred to in your statement, you only know about them from the stories of other people.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1746
utterances.text: I am fortunate not to have seen a killing.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You are fortunate because of that, but I'm saying that you never saw a killing yourself.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1746
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I think -- just a moment. We will now go into private session, and, Mr. Milosevic -- Mr. Milosevic, we will consider whether you should have any time longer because your time is now up.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, we are in public session.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let us not argue about it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will not even refer to the town, Mr. May.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Or anywhere else that she went.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Or anywhere else that she went, only the fact that she went to Serbia, which I suppose does not identify her.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So is it true that you stayed with the family of your husband in Serbia, in a town?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1746
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is it true that the family of your husband were also Muslims?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1746
utterances.text: The woman was Muslim, and the man was Serb.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But they were family of your husband.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1746
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And those relatives of yours lived peacefully in Serbia, and they were able and they could afford to receive refugees from Bosnia and Herzegovina, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1746
utterances.text: They could not really afford to. We had to take care of ourselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So nobody in Serbia had any doubts that you were Muslims in that place where you stayed.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1746
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did anybody harm you in any way because of that fact?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1746
utterances.text: No, not at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that there were 70.000 Muslim refugees in Serbia at the time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1746
utterances.text: I know that there were refugees. I don't know exactly how many right now. But I also know that there was a number of Muslims who were detained in Serbia, specifically from Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Nobody was detained there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, this is your last question now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Mrs. 1746, did the authorities of the Republic of Serbia help you get the documents that enabled you to travel on to a third country? Can we conclude that your family, yourself, and other Muslims from Bosnia and Herzegovina who were escaping the war in Bosnia-Herzegovina found refuge and shelter precisely in Serbia and received there the necessary assistance enabling you to travel on? Is that disputable?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1746
utterances.text: I didn't say that we were mistreated or that we did not receive help. I only want to say that I was there myself, Mr. Milosevic, and I was disappointed in your media, and at one point I regretted that I was a Muslim because, watching your news bulletins on the TV and listening to the radio, I heard about Muslims allegedly killing Serbs in Bosnia and alleged mass graves of Serb civilians being discovered in Bosnia. I had been on both sides, and I'm really sorry that I ended up thinking that it was to be regretted that I belonged to either of these nations, either of these ethnic groups. That's what you flooded the population of Serbia with.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You think that information was untrue?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1746
utterances.text: That information was absolutely untrue, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Just one brief matter in private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Private session, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, we are in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Witness, this is a draft of the first statement that was taken from you in April 2000. It's in English. Does your signature appear on any of the pages of that statement?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1746
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: That statement wasn't read back to you on the first occasion in your own language?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1746
utterances.text: No, it was not read out to me in detail. It was not read out to me, not this statement. I'm sorry. Let me add that we were supposed to make another appointment to finalise this and have me sign the statement because the computer had stopped working.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And it was on the second occasion you were seen by members of the Office of the Prosecutor in 2002, April 2002, that you went back through your evidence, made some changes, and then signed the English version of the statement that was read back to you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1746
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, precisely. And we corrected at the same time the errors that were found in the first version. We corrected them together.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: Your Honours, just a brief point of confusion. Perhaps it was my confusion. The second statement doesn't identify the White Eagles as Arkan's White Eagles, that's again something that appears in the first draft. And very briefly one additional matter. Could the witness please be referred, please, to the second statement in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Look, please, at paragraph 21 of that statement. Witness, you identify Red Berets as being present at the JNA barracks in early April, from early April 1992. The other paramilitaries that you have described, where did you see their base, or did you see where they were based?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B-1746
utterances.text: The Red Berets were at the garrison within the compound of the garrison, whereas White Eagles were scattered around the houses we had vacated. They were around before I left the village and went to town.

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: No further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Witness B-1746, that concludes your evidence. Thank you for coming to the International Tribunal to give it. You are free to go. If you would just wait for the blinds to be drawn.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Agha, is it for you to call the next witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. The Prosecution calls Mr. Esad Velic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. If someone would draw these blinds, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: Your Honour, this witness has facial protection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: While the witness is coming in, may I answer the accused's concern about audio versions of intercepts. He was provided them on the 23rd of October on a CD. If he has trouble with following the method of opening them, one of my staff will help him at the end of the session.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: Your Honours, while we're waiting for the next witness, could I please address a point of the exhibit photograph of the camp which the accused drew our attention to. This was Exhibit 597, tab 4, and it was a picture of the inside of a hangar. I have been able to find out that that picture was actually taken by a delegation from the CSCE, which was the forerunner to the OSCE, in the end of August, September 1992. So that's for the information of the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I don't have the picture with me now, but some of the detainees wore uniforms at the time? The right hand part of the picture. If you check it later.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: It would seem so, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And some of the detainees are dressed up, and some wore neckties?

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: There are not many with neckties.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just a moment. Let the witness take the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If you would like to take a seat.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, if it is about the neckties in the last photograph, we'll deal with it at the end. Let us hear this witness now.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: Your Honours, this is a 92 bis witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: Witness, you gave a statement before the Office of the Prosecution on the 31st of October, 1999, which was subsequently certified by members of the Registry on the 31st of May, 2001. You have that statement in front of you. Can you confirm that that is in fact your signature and your statement, please.

utterances.speaker: ESAD VELIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is my signature and that is my statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: May I ask that statement be given an exhibit number, the bis package.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The next exhibit number is 599.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, Your Honours, this witness is from again a different municipality on which no evidence has yet been led, so if I may very briefly ask you to refer to Exhibit 343, 1, where the witness can kindly please point out on that exhibit on the ELMO the municipality of Bosanska Krupa, where he's from.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: Witness, could you please point on the ELMO there whereabouts Bosanska Krupa is on the map of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: ESAD VELIC
utterances.text: [Indicates]

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you very much, Witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. AGHA
utterances.text: Your Honours, because we are rather short of time, I propose to briefly skim through the summarisation of this witness's testimony. Now, the witness, in 1990, was living in Bosanska Krupa, and prior to the multi-party elections he became a member of the SDA. Bosanska Krupa is a 75 per cent Muslim majority municipality, and the SDA won a majority of seats. He then became the first elected president of Bosanska Krupa. The main difficulty with the SDS party concerned the JNA's involvement in Croatia. The SDA didn't want the JNA to be involved, whereas the SDS did. This led to a confrontation and a demand from the SDS to see the personnel detail of the JNA's conscripts in the area. The SDA didn't allow this, and this led to the JNA attempting to seize the documents. The SDS then prepared a study of the administrative division of the municipality, and the study was based on a separate ethnic state for the Serbs. The main justification for the SDS wanting a separate municipality was that they could no longer live with the persons who had committed crimes against them during World War II, and this separation would be the first step in creating a Serbian state in the Balkans. Now, the witness also deals with the arrest of Martic and him being released after the arrest warrants were revoked from Belgrade and that Martic met Mladic straight after his release. Concerning the attack on Bosanska Krupa, this occurred just after a meeting on 21st of April, 1992, when a meeting was held in the municipal building attended by EU monitors, himself, who were going to discuss the various controversies. A JNA general, Ninkovic, came in the meeting, and about 15 minutes after he left the town was shelled as well as shot at by Serbian forces. Very briefly, the witness was in the municipal building, and he did see about 25 to 30 casualties. Bosanska Krupa is divided by the River Una, and on account of the Serb shelling, the Muslims were forced to the left bank. Later on, the witness noticed that nearly all the houses had been destroyed, including the mosque and the Catholic church on the side which the Serbs were occupying. So that's in essence the testimony of this witness and I have no further questions or exhibits to run through him. That ends of the examination-in-chief, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Have I understood this correctly, Mr. May? This witness only has facial protection. His name is not protected? I can address him by his name, can't I?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That is so.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Velic, I see from your statement that before the conflict broke out in Bosnia-Herzegovina, you held many important offices in the territory of the municipality of Bosanska Krupa. You were a judge of the municipal court, the public prosecutor, a magistrate, head of the 4th of July Company. According to my information, for a while you were a public self-management attorney; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ESAD VELIC
utterances.text: No, it's not right. I was never a magistrate, and I was never the public defender. I was the district public attorney for three years, though.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: As soon as the SDA was established, you became a member of the Executive Board of the SDA for Bosanska Krupa; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ESAD VELIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And in September 1991, at the internal elections of the SDA, you were elected president of the SDA in Bosanska Krupa; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: ESAD VELIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And now, Mr. Velic, when you talk about party activities in the territory of your municipality in the period that preceded the conflict, first of all, on page 2, in paragraph 9 you talk about the founding Assembly of the SDS, and then on page 3, in paragraph 1, you say that the SDA had its founding Assembly on the 31st of July, 1990. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ESAD VELIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: While following your statement, one could come to the wrong conclusion that it was the SDS that was founded first and then the SDA, which certainly was not the case; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ESAD VELIC
utterances.text: I never said that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: When was the SDA established in relation to the SDS? How much earlier?

utterances.speaker: ESAD VELIC
utterances.text: Perhaps a month or two earlier, but I don't know exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. In view of the fact that you were invited as a guest to the founding Assembly of the Serb Democratic Party --

utterances.speaker: ESAD VELIC
utterances.text: Well, I was not invited myself, but representatives of the SDA were invited, and we agreed that I would attend inter alia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. They did not invite you by name and surname, but they asked -- they invited the representatives of the leadership of the SDA to attend the founding Assembly of the SDS.

utterances.speaker: ESAD VELIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Then you were appointed to go on behalf of the SDA to attend the founding Assembly of the SDS.

utterances.speaker: ESAD VELIC
utterances.text: Others attended too, but I was the one who took it upon myself to address this founding Assembly with a short statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. And on which date was this founding Assembly of the SDS held?

utterances.speaker: ESAD VELIC
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. And what was the content of this short statement that you made when addressing the founding Assembly of the Serb Democratic Party?

utterances.speaker: ESAD VELIC
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, it was a courtesy statement, extending greetings, and I expressed my hope that the parties of the two peoples would find a common language in terms of resolving Bosnian affairs.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. You were born in a village which was in the biggest local commune in Bosanska Krupa.

utterances.speaker: ESAD VELIC
utterances.text: No, Maglic is not in the area of Buzim. It never belonged to the municipality of Buzim but the municipality of Bosanska Krupa.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Was Buzim a municipality then or was it a local commune within Bosanska Krupa?

utterances.speaker: ESAD VELIC
utterances.text: Well, it was a local commune within the municipality of Bosanska Krupa.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: ESAD VELIC
utterances.text: But organisationally, they were separate or, rather, the SDA organisations were different. There were two SDA organisations in the territory of the municipality of Bosanska Krupa, one for Buzim and one for Bosanska Krupa.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Oh, I see, although this was a single municipality. And since 1995 these were separate municipalities?

utterances.speaker: ESAD VELIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I found out later, towards the end of 1995, that Buzim acquired the status of a proper municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that Buzim was almost completely populated by Muslims, namely since the Second World War when several thousand Serbs in Buzim were killed and expelled from the area?

utterances.speaker: ESAD VELIC
utterances.text: In Buzim or, rather, in the community of the municipality of Buzim, that included seven local communes as far as I can remember, for the most part the population was Muslim in 1999. I cannot corroborate your statement that during the Second World War several thousand Serbs were expelled from that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
